strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across six benchmarks, three domains, and multiple models with strong token reduction results (29.68% on GAIA)
Well-designed ablation studies (Table 3) clearly showing contributions of each component (correction, guidance, purification)
Practical modularity: non-intrusive design allows integration into existing MAS architectures without core modifications
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and thorough implementation details including full prompts in appendix
Addresses important real-world problem of balancing robustness and efficiency in complex multi-agent systems
Demonstrates variance reduction (63% on Level 2) suggesting more predictable and reliable performance
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core concept (meta-agent supervision) is very similar to existing AWorld Guard agent; differentiation is insufficiently justified with only one comparison experiment on 30 GAIA tasks

Heuristic-based adaptive filter (checking for specific strings, 3000-char threshold) is brittle and design choices lack principled justification; questionable generalization to other MAS architectures
Incomplete cost-benefit analysis: paper doesn't account for LLM tokens consumed by supervision decisions; claims LLM-free filter but subsequent corrections/guidance/verifications require LLM calls
Observation purification trade-offs underexplored: paper acknowledges accuracy drops but doesn't deeply analyze when purification helps vs. hurts (MBPP -1.25%, DROP -1.28% F1 not discussed)
Smolagent-centric evaluation limiting generalizability: testbed chosen specifically because it avoids external tools, but modern high-performing agents heavily rely on APIs; results may not transfer
Level-dependent inconsistency unexplained: token reduction ranges from 7.69% (L3) to 34.64% (L2) to 13.48% (L1) without analysis of why supervision helps more on certain difficulty levels
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; small datasets (AIME ~60 examples) reported without uncertainty quantification
Insufficient engagement with related work: no direct comparison with context compression methods (Chen et al., Mou et al.), agent dropout, or other efficiency approaches mentioned in Related Work
Definition 1 (SMAS) is generic and post-hoc rather than driving methodology; formalism provides limited insights
Incomplete ablations: Table 3 uses only top-10 most expensive tasks per level (30 total) rather than full GAIA set; no ablation of filter components

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing real deployment concerns in MAS efficiency and robustness
Comprehensive experimental validation: 6 benchmarks, 3+ foundation models, 3 MAS frameworks with consistent ~30% token reduction
Clear conceptual framework with formal definitions (SMAS) and well-structured methodology (What/When/How)
Clever LLM-free adaptive filter design that avoids prohibitive supervision overhead while enabling targeted interventions
Non-intrusive modular architecture that works across different MAS frameworks without modification (demonstrated on Smolagent, AWorld, OAgents)
Thorough ablation studies quantifying individual component contributions; performance consistency demonstrated with statistical metrics (variance reduction)
Excellent presentation with detailed implementation appendix, concrete case studies, and transparent discussion of insights and limitations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core intervention strategies (error correction, guidance, observation cleaning) are intuitive engineering solutions rather than fundamental innovations
Adaptive filter design lacks principled foundation: thresholds (e.g., 3000-char limit) appear arbitrary; detection heuristics underspecified; no sensitivity analysis of filter design choices
Evaluation testbed bias: deliberate focus on Smolagent's internal reasoning avoids realistic scenarios where external APIs dominate, limiting generalizability of efficiency claims
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests despite claiming ~30% improvements
Incomplete accuracy-efficiency analysis: Table 2 shows non-trivial accuracy drops (MBPP -1.25%, DROP -1.28%) not adequately explained or addressed
Prompts and engineering quality concerns: lengthy task-specific prompts (A.5) raise questions about prompt engineering vs. fundamental contribution; no ablation on prompt sensitivity
Insufficient failure mode analysis: when does SUPERVISORAGENT fail? Which agent/task types benefit most? Largely unexamined
Supervisor overhead not quantified: no analysis of tokens consumed by SUPERVISORAGENT itself or latency impact of supervision
Limited baseline comparisons: other efficiency-focused methods (MetaAgent, SafeSieve) mentioned but not experimentally compared under identical conditions

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear formalization of Supervised Multi-Agent Systems, articulating genuine challenges in modern MAS complexity
Pragmatic technical design with LLM-free adaptive filter that avoids recursive supervision overhead while enabling graduated intervention intensity
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 benchmarks, multiple foundation models (GPT-4.1, Gemini, Qwen3), and cross-framework validation (Smolagent, OAgents, AWorld)
Strong and consistent empirical results showing 29.68% average token reduction on GAIA, with particularly effective performance on hard tasks (34.64% on Level 2) and 63% variance reduction
Thorough ablation study isolating component contributions and detailed transparency with full implementation details, hyperparameters, and overhead analysis (15.45% net supervisor cost)
Honest reporting of trade-offs including accuracy drops on some benchmarks and 37% latency overhead, with failure mode analysis in appendix
Non-intrusive architecture enabling application to existing MAS frameworks without modification, demonstrating versatility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—combines established techniques (error correction, observation filtering) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts; distinction from similar approaches like Guard agents understated

Heuristic-based adaptive filter lacks principled foundation with hand-crafted thresholds requiring manual tuning; hyperparameters vary significantly across benchmarks (Table 5) with limited guidance for new domains; sensitivity analysis only examines one parameter on one benchmark

Accuracy trade-offs inadequately analyzed—Table 2 shows drops (DROP: 81.08%→79.80%, MBPP: 85.68%→84.43%) attributed to over-compression but not systematically investigated; noise-as-signal phenomenon mentioned briefly but deserves deeper analysis

Non-trivial latency overhead (37.27% average increase, ~90 seconds per task) understated as justifiable trade-off; purification drives most latency cost, creating tension with efficiency goals; time-sensitive application implications not discussed

No empirical comparison with related efficiency-focused methods (AgentDropout, SafeSieve, context compression) despite claiming orthogonality; evaluation limited to established benchmarks without validation of complementarity

Limited generalization—all evaluations on static task-solving benchmarks without truly multi-agent coordination scenarios; framework applicability unclear for dynamic/interactive or embodied AI domains; title suggests broader scope than demonstrated

Insufficient failure mode analysis—three modes identified (A.5) with limited empirical quantification; hard constraint of 2 guidance interventions appears arbitrary; performance degradation on weaker models (Qwen3-235B) not thoroughly explored

Incomplete evaluation metrics—focuses on token/accuracy; missing false positive rates of filter, per-intervention cost-benefit analysis, and breakdown of overhead distribution; robustness defined as variance reduction rather than safety guarantees

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across 6 benchmarks, 3 foundation models, and 3 MAS frameworks with detailed ablation studies and overhead analysis
Strong empirical results on primary GAIA benchmark (29.68% token reduction at pass@1, up to 50.13% on complex subsets) with maintained or improved accuracy
Practical modular design that doesn't require modifying base agent architectures, enabling adoption on existing systems
Thorough implementation details, prompts, and case studies supporting reproducibility and understanding
Principled formal framework (SMAS, context window, action space) combined with efficient LLM-free adaptive filter for practical efficiency
Reduction in token cost variance (63% on GAIA Level 2) addresses important reliability concern beyond just average performance
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: supervisory agents in multi-agent systems are not new; individual components (error correction, guidance, purification) are straightforward LLM applications; main contribution is packaging/integration rather than novel methodology

Heuristic-based adaptive filter requires manual tuning with benchmark-specific hyperparameters (τ_len=3000 for Smolagent, 10000 for OAgents), limiting generalizability and requiring manual calibration for new scenarios

Inconsistent improvements across benchmarks: strong on GAIA and HumanEval but only 5.60% on DROP and 6.62% on MBPP, suggesting optimization to specific task structures without clear characterization of when method succeeds

Substantial latency overhead (37.27% average increase, ~90 seconds per task) not adequately justified; for many real-world applications, latency is as critical as token cost but treated as secondary concern

Model-agnosticism claims overstated: failure mode analysis reveals variance in trigger frequency across models, with less capable models triggering correction significantly more often, increasing overhead and undermining claimed generality

Missing direct empirical comparisons with related supervisory approaches (e.g., Guard in AWorld); baselines for some domains seem weak; no comparison with other efficiency techniques mentioned in related work

Insufficient analysis of when/why method works: limited investigation of task characteristics benefiting most from supervision; single case study insufficient; no systematic characterization of success factors

Quantification of failure modes incomplete: information loss during purification not measured; hard cutoff on guidance interventions (max 2) appears ad-hoc; scalability to larger MAS systems unexplored
Code availability statement incomplete (blank link); hyperparameter selection process for different benchmarks not fully documented; prompt design iteration/ablation not discussed
